```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# Run from this project folder; data are supplied separately.
root <- normalizePath('.', winslash='/')
library(data.table)
library(ranger)
library(xgboost)
library(e1071)
library(jsonlite)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo=TRUE,message=FALSE,warning=TRUE,error=FALSE,
                     fig.width=6.3,fig.height=3.7,dpi=180)
options(width=90,digits=5,scipen=8)
setDTthreads(4)
results <- file.path(root,'results')
dir.create(results,showWarnings=FALSE,recursive=TRUE)
seed <- 691006L
# Define identical evaluation measures for every probability forecast.
loss <- function(y,p) {p<-pmin(pmax(p,1e-15),1-1e-15);-mean(y*log(p)+(1-y)*log(1-p))}
auc <- function(y,p) {n1<-sum(y==1);n0<-sum(y==0);(sum(rank(p)[y==1])-n1*(n1+1)/2)/(n1*n0)}
measure <- function(y,p,cut=.5) {
 z<-as.integer(p>=cut);tp<-sum(z==1 & y==1);tn<-sum(z==0 & y==0)
 fp<-sum(z==1 & y==0);fn<-sum(z==0 & y==1)
 pr<-if(tp+fp)tp/(tp+fp) else 0;re<-tp/(tp+fn)
 c(Log_loss=loss(y,p),AUC=auc(y,p),Accuracy=mean(z==y),Precision=pr,Recall=re,
   F1=if(pr+re)2*pr*re/(pr+re) else 0,TP=tp,TN=tn,FP=fp,FN=fn)
}
tab <- function(x,digits=4) knitr::kable(x,digits=digits,row.names=FALSE)
```

# Purpose and main finding

I compared the selected logistic regression, SVM, Random Forest, and XGBoost specifications from Weeks 3 through 5. The earlier scores came from different samples and selection criteria. I therefore refitted the four specifications using one common training sample and evaluated them on identical labeled customers. The comparison uses binary log loss as the shared cost measure and reports accuracy at the same 0.50 cutoff. I also examine AUC, recall, and F1 because a classifier can get about 90% accuracy here by predicting every customer as negative.

```{r data-checks}
# Use the labeled course file, never the unlabeled Kaggle customer test file.
data_path <- file.path(root,'data','train.csv')
dat <- fread(data_path)
features <- grep('^var_',names(dat),value=TRUE)
stopifnot(nrow(dat)==200000L,length(features)==200L,
          all(dat$target %in% 0:1),!anyDuplicated(dat$ID_code))
checks <- data.frame(Customers=nrow(dat),Predictors=length(features),
 Positive=sum(dat$target),Positive_percent=100*mean(dat$target),Missing_cells=sum(is.na(dat)))
tab(checks)
```

# Data preparation and comparison design

The response is the binary `target` variable. The 200 anonymized numerical fields are potential predictors; `ID_code` is retained only for auditing. There are 20,098 positive customers, or 10.049% of the labeled data. The variables have no supplied business meanings, so an association with `var_81`, for example, cannot be described as a specific customer behavior.

```{r common-split}
# Reserve 20% of each class for validation and a separate 20% for testing.
# Keep all four algorithms on exactly 6,000 common fitting rows, matching
# the earlier SVM resource budget instead of giving the forests more rows.
set.seed(seed)
fit_idx<-val_idx<-test_idx<-integer()
for(cl in 0:1) {
 ids<-sample(which(dat$target==cl)); n<-length(ids); nv<-floor(.2*n)
 val_idx<-c(val_idx,ids[seq_len(nv)])
 test_idx<-c(test_idx,ids[nv+seq_len(nv)])
 pool<-ids[(2*nv+1L):n]
 nf<-if(cl==1)603L else 5397L
 fit_idx<-c(fit_idx,pool[seq_len(nf)])
}
stopifnot(!length(intersect(fit_idx,val_idx)),!length(intersect(fit_idx,test_idx)),
          !length(intersect(val_idx,test_idx)))
# Learn imputation and scaling from fitting rows only.
x<-as.matrix(dat[,..features]);y<-dat$target
med<-apply(x[fit_idx,,drop=FALSE],2,median,na.rm=TRUE)
stopifnot(all(is.finite(med)))
for(j in seq_along(features)) x[is.na(x[,j]),j]<-med[j]
center<-colMeans(x[fit_idx,,drop=FALSE]);spread<-apply(x[fit_idx,,drop=FALSE],2,sd)
stopifnot(all(is.finite(spread)),all(spread>0))
z<-scale(x,center=center,scale=spread)
membership<-rep('Not used for fitting or evaluation',nrow(dat))
membership[fit_idx]<-'Training';membership[val_idx]<-'Validation';membership[test_idx]<-'Test'
fwrite(data.table(ID_code=dat$ID_code,Partition=membership),file.path(results,'split_membership.csv'))
split_table<-data.frame(Partition=c('Training','Validation','Test','Unused'),
 Rows=c(length(fit_idx),length(val_idx),length(test_idx),sum(grepl('Not used',membership))),
 Positive=c(sum(y[fit_idx]),sum(y[val_idx]),sum(y[test_idx]),sum(y[grepl('Not used',membership)])))
split_table$Positive_percent<-100*split_table$Positive/split_table$Rows
tab(split_table)
# Reuse completed fits only when code, input data, packages, and split IDs match.
# Delete verified_execution_cache.rds to force all four models to refit.
signature<-list(code=unname(tools::md5sum(file.path(root,'analysis.Rmd'))),
 data=unname(tools::md5sum(data_path)),seed=seed,fit=fit_idx,val=val_idx,test=test_idx,
 versions=sapply(c('ranger','e1071','xgboost'),function(p)as.character(packageVersion(p))))
cache_file<-file.path(results,'verified_execution_cache.rds')
cached<-if(file.exists(cache_file))readRDS(cache_file) else NULL
use_cache<-!is.null(cached) && identical(cached$signature,signature)
```

The common fitting sample contains 6,000 customers, including 603 positives. Validation and test each contain `r length(val_idx)` customers. The remaining rows are not used. This deliberately controls training volume across algorithms and keeps the SVM computation practical. It also means the new forest and boosting scores are not replacements for Week 5's full-data results: those models previously had 119,999 training rows.

The fixed seed is 691006. Imputation medians, scaling means, and standard deviations come only from the fitting sample. Logistic regression and SVM use standardized predictors; trees use the original numerical scales. Only logistic regression screens predictors, using correlations computed on the fitting rows.

The validation partition is used for SVM probability calibration and optional cutoff selection. The test partition is excluded from those operations and from fitting. However, these are previously studied course data, not an independent external dataset. Prior model choices already reflect earlier experiments on this file. The new split supports a consistent internal comparison, not a claim of completely new external validation.

# Selected models from earlier weeks

Week 3 selected a top-50 linear logistic model by validation AUC after comparing an intercept-only model, smaller linear models, squared terms, and interactions. Week 4 selected the balanced radial SVM M09 by validation AUC. Week 5 selected RF06 and XGB03 by validation log loss. I retain those specifications instead of changing them after seeing this week's test outcomes.

The earlier logistic report recorded validation AUC 0.8057 and log loss 0.2606 on 50,001 validation customers after fitting 149,999 training rows. The selected SVM recorded validation AUC 0.8596 with 6,000 fitting rows and 4,000 validation rows. RF06 and XGB03 recorded validation log losses of 0.26904 and 0.21188, respectively, after fitting 119,999 rows and validating on 39,999 rows. Those historical values describe the earlier exercises; I do not rank all four algorithms by those mismatched samples.

```{r final-settings}
# Store every final fitting choice explicitly rather than relying on defaults.
settings<-data.frame(Algorithm=c('Logistic regression','SVM','Random Forest','XGBoost'),
 Prior_choice=c('Top 50 linear','M09','RF06','XGB03'),
 Final_settings=c('Binomial logit; intercept; 50 screened linear predictors; no penalty; maxit 50',
 'Radial C classification; C 0.01; gamma 0.005; inverse frequency class weights; tolerance 0.001',
 'Probability forest; 500 trees; mtry 40; min.node.size 30; Gini; bootstrap fraction 1',
 'Binary logistic; depth 4; eta 0.10; 600 rounds; subsample 1; colsample 1; min child weight 1; lambda 1; alpha 0; gamma 0; hist'))
tab(settings)
```

Logistic regression has no tree depth, C, or learning rate. Its selected model complexity is 50 additive predictors, with an intercept and no interactions or squared terms. Its binomial logit coefficients are fitted by maximum likelihood with up to 50 iterations.

For the SVM, class weights equal the training sample size divided by twice each class count: `r round(6000/(2*5397),5)` for class 0 and `r round(6000/(2*603),5)` for class 1. The radial kernel is `exp(-gamma * squared_distance)`. Standardizing inputs keeps differences in numerical scale from dominating that distance. I preserve the signed decision-score classifier from Week 4 and add a separate validation-based logistic calibration so its forecasts can be compared with other probabilities using log loss.

For the forest, `min.node.size=30` controls when splitting stops; it does not guarantee 30 records in every leaf. Bootstrap sampling uses replacement, with a sample fraction of 1. XGBoost retains the 600 rounds selected in Week 5. I do not use this week's test results to extend that search. Every fit uses the same seed and four threads where supported.

# Cost functions and their interpretation

Binary log loss is the negative mean of `y*log(p) + (1-y)*log(1-p)`, using natural logarithms. Lower values mean the model assigns more probability to the observed outcomes. A confidently wrong forecast is penalized more heavily than an uncertain one. I clip probabilities only at 1e-15 and 1 minus 1e-15 to avoid undefined logarithms.

Logistic regression minimizes negative binomial log likelihood. For the unweighted model here, training residual deviance is twice the total negative log likelihood. The SVM instead minimizes half the squared boundary norm plus C times the weighted sum of hinge losses, where each hinge loss is the larger of zero and one minus the signed margin. Its C value is a penalty multiplier, not the reported predictive loss. A decision score is not itself a probability.

Random Forest reduces weighted Gini impurity at each split and averages leaf probabilities. It does not directly optimize a global log-loss objective. XGBoost fits additional trees to gradients and Hessians of logistic loss, with leaf-count and leaf-weight penalties. Eta shrinks each update. Its displayed log-loss history excludes regularization penalties.

These native objectives use different scales and cannot be ranked as one interchangeable cost function. I compare the final forecasts using the same unweighted held-out log loss. Percentage cost reduction is 100 times the difference between the constant-forecast loss and model loss, divided by constant loss. No bank-specific prices for false positives or false negatives are supplied, so none of these numbers represents dollars saved.

```{r fit-logistic}
# Rank associations only inside the common fitting sample and retain 50 fields.
correlations<-apply(z[fit_idx,,drop=FALSE],2,function(v)cor(v,y[fit_idx]))
top50<-names(sort(abs(correlations),decreasing=TRUE))[1:50]
logistic_frame<-data.frame(target=y[fit_idx],z[fit_idx,top50,drop=FALSE])
logistic_fit<-if(use_cache)cached$models$logistic else glm(target~.,data=logistic_frame,family=binomial(),
                  control=glm.control(maxit=50))
stopifnot(logistic_fit$converged,all(is.finite(coef(logistic_fit))))
lp<-function(idx)as.numeric(predict(logistic_fit,newdata=data.frame(z[idx,top50,drop=FALSE]),type='response'))
fwrite(data.table(Predictor=top50,Training_correlation=correlations[top50]),file.path(results,'logistic_predictors.csv'))
cat('Logistic model converged:',logistic_fit$converged,'\nPredictors:',length(top50),'\n')
```

```{r fit-svm}
# Fit the previously selected SVM on the same rows as all other algorithms.
weights<-6000/(2*table(factor(y[fit_idx],levels=0:1)))
set.seed(seed)
svm_fit<-if(use_cache)cached$models$svm else svm(x=z[fit_idx,,drop=FALSE],y=factor(y[fit_idx],levels=0:1),
 type='C-classification',kernel='radial',cost=.01,gamma=.005,
 class.weights=weights,scale=FALSE,probability=FALSE,tolerance=.001,
 cachesize=400,shrinking=TRUE)
# Orient the raw margin toward class 1 using the libsvm level convention.
score<-function(idx) {
 pred<-predict(svm_fit,z[idx,,drop=FALSE],decision.values=TRUE)
 raw<-as.numeric(attr(pred,'decision.values'))
 if(svm_fit$levels[svm_fit$labels[1]]=='1')raw else -raw
}
# Cache includes scores in the verified partition order to avoid costly reruns.
if(use_cache) {
 s_train<-cached$margins$train;s_val<-cached$margins$validation;s_test<-cached$margins$test
} else {s_train<-score(fit_idx);s_val<-score(val_idx);s_test<-score(test_idx)}
# Fit a two-coefficient probability mapping only on validation observations.
calibration<-glm(outcome~margin,data=data.frame(outcome=y[val_idx],margin=s_val),family=binomial())
stopifnot(calibration$converged,all(is.finite(coef(calibration))))
sp<-function(s)as.numeric(predict(calibration,newdata=data.frame(margin=s),type='response'))
tab(data.frame(Term=names(coef(calibration)),Coefficient=as.numeric(coef(calibration))))
cat('Support vectors:',svm_fit$tot.nSV,'\n')
```

The SVM calibration fits an intercept and a slope to validation scores and binary outcomes. It changes the probability scale without refitting the SVM boundary. Its validation log loss is a calibration-fit diagnostic, not an independent evaluation of the calibrated model. The common test results provide the held-out check. Logistic regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost are not recalibrated here; that is a limitation of the comparison.

```{r fit-random-forest}
# Refit RF06 with the frozen Week 5 settings and identical fitting rows.
rf_fit<-if(use_cache)cached$models$forest else ranger(x=x[fit_idx,,drop=FALSE],y=factor(y[fit_idx],levels=0:1),
 probability=TRUE,num.trees=500,mtry=40,min.node.size=30,splitrule='gini',
 replace=TRUE,sample.fraction=1,importance='none',num.threads=4,seed=seed)
rp<-function(idx)as.numeric(predict(rf_fit,x[idx,,drop=FALSE],num.threads=4)$predictions[,'1'])
cat('Forest trees:',rf_fit$num.trees,'\nmtry:',rf_fit$mtry,'\n')
```

```{r fit-xgboost}
# Fit exactly the prior selected 600 rounds, without test-based early stopping.
xgb_params<-list(objective='binary:logistic',eval_metric='logloss',max_depth=4,
 eta=.1,subsample=1,colsample_bytree=1,min_child_weight=1,lambda=1,alpha=0,
 gamma=0,tree_method='hist',nthread=4,seed=seed,scale_pos_weight=1,max_bin=256)
dtrain<-xgb.DMatrix(x[fit_idx,,drop=FALSE],label=y[fit_idx])
dval<-xgb.DMatrix(x[val_idx,,drop=FALSE],label=y[val_idx])
if(use_cache && !is.null(cached$history) && nrow(cached$history)==600L) {
 xgb_fit<-xgb.load(file.path(results,'xgboost.ubj'))
 xgb_history<-cached$history
} else {
 xgb_fit<-xgb.train(params=xgb_params,data=dtrain,nrounds=600,
  evals=list(train=dtrain,validation=dval),verbose=0)
 # XGBoost 3.2 stores evaluation history as an R attribute, not a list field.
 xgb_history<-as.data.frame(attr(xgb_fit,'evaluation_log'))
}
xp<-function(idx)as.numeric(predict(xgb_fit,xgb.DMatrix(x[idx,,drop=FALSE])))
stopifnot(nrow(xgb_history)==600L,all(c('train_logloss','validation_logloss') %in% names(xgb_history)))
cat('Boosting rounds:',nrow(xgb_history),'\n')
```

# Common evaluation results

```{r cost-and-accuracy}
# Collect probabilities in the same row order for each shared partition.
probs_train<-list(Logistic=lp(fit_idx),SVM=sp(s_train),Random_Forest=rp(fit_idx),XGBoost=xp(fit_idx))
probs_val<-list(Logistic=lp(val_idx),SVM=sp(s_val),Random_Forest=rp(val_idx),XGBoost=xp(val_idx))
probs_test<-list(Logistic=lp(test_idx),SVM=sp(s_test),Random_Forest=rp(test_idx),XGBoost=xp(test_idx))
base_probability<-mean(y[fit_idx]);base_test<-loss(y[test_idx],rep(base_probability,length(test_idx)))
test_table<-rbindlist(lapply(names(probs_test),function(n) {
 p<-probs_test[[n]];stopifnot(length(p)==length(test_idx),all(is.finite(p)),all(p>=0 & p<=1))
 as.data.table(c(list(Model=n),as.list(measure(y[test_idx],p,.5))))
}))
test_table[,Reduction_percent:=100*(base_test-Log_loss)/base_test]
cost_table<-data.frame(Model=names(probs_test),
 Training_loss=sapply(probs_train,function(p)loss(y[fit_idx],p)),
 Validation_loss=sapply(probs_val,function(p)loss(y[val_idx],p)),
 Test_loss=test_table$Log_loss,Test_reduction_percent=test_table$Reduction_percent)
tab(cost_table)
tab(test_table[,.(Model,Accuracy,AUC,Precision,Recall,F1)])
winner<-test_table$Model[which.min(test_table$Log_loss)]
accuracy_winner<-test_table$Model[which.max(test_table$Accuracy)]
```

The lowest test log loss belongs to `r winner`, at `r sprintf('%.5f',min(test_table$Log_loss))`. That is `r sprintf('%.2f',max(test_table$Reduction_percent))`% below the constant forecast's `r sprintf('%.5f',base_test)` loss. The highest test accuracy at 0.50 belongs to `r accuracy_winner`, at `r sprintf('%.2f',100*max(test_table$Accuracy))`%. These conclusions are restricted to the four frozen specifications and the common 6,000-row training budget.

The always-negative baseline has `r sprintf('%.2f',100*mean(y[test_idx]==0))`% test accuracy and zero recall. Accuracy must therefore be read alongside the positive-class measures. The cost table also separates in-sample training fit from held-out outcomes. A very low training loss can indicate memorization if the test loss remains much higher. The SVM's validation loss is especially optimistic because calibration was fitted there.

XGBoost illustrates that warning in this run. Its training loss is only `r sprintf('%.5f',cost_table$Training_loss[cost_table$Model=='XGBoost'])`, but its test loss is `r sprintf('%.5f',test_table[Model=='XGBoost',Log_loss])`, which is `r sprintf('%.2f',-test_table[Model=='XGBoost',Reduction_percent])`% worse than the constant forecast. Keeping 600 rounds after reducing the training sample to 6,000 customers leads to overly confident predictions. This does not contradict the stronger Week 5 result with 119,999 training rows. Random Forest also struggles at 0.50, finding `r test_table[Model=='Random_Forest',TP]` positive customers while missing `r test_table[Model=='Random_Forest',FN]`. Its probabilities still improve log loss over the constant forecast, but that cutoff is ineffective for finding positives.

```{r cost-accuracy-graph}
# Display shared predictive cost and accuracy in separate, labeled panels.
par(mfrow=c(1,2),mar=c(7,4,2,1))
labels<-c('Logistic','SVM','Forest','XGBoost')
barplot(test_table$Log_loss,names.arg=labels,las=2,col='gray65',ylim=c(0,max(base_test,test_table$Log_loss)*1.15),
 ylab='Test binary log loss',main='Probability cost')
abline(h=base_test,lty=2);legend('topright','Constant forecast',lty=2,bty='n',cex=.75)
barplot(100*test_table$Accuracy,names.arg=labels,las=2,col='steelblue',ylim=c(0,100),
 ylab='Test accuracy percent',main='Cutoff 0.50')
abline(h=100*mean(y[test_idx]==0),lty=2)
par(mfrow=c(1,1))
```

The left panel compares probability cost, where shorter bars are better. Its dashed line is the constant-probability forecast. The right panel compares accuracy at 0.50, where taller bars are better. Its dashed line is the always-negative baseline. The panels use different units and should not be read as a common scale. A small accuracy gain can coexist with a substantial reduction in log loss because one measures thresholded decisions and the other evaluates confidence.

# Confusion matrices and cutoff tradeoffs

```{r confusion-matrices}
# Show all four outcomes for each model at the identical 0.50 threshold.
tab(test_table[,.(Model,TP,TN,FP,FN)],digits=0)
# Select an optional F1 cutoff on validation only, never using test labels.
cutoffs<-sapply(probs_val,function(p) {
 grid<-seq(.01,.80,.01);f<-sapply(grid,function(t)measure(y[val_idx],p,t)['F1'])
 grid[which.max(f)]
})
cutoff_table<-rbindlist(lapply(names(probs_test),function(n)
 as.data.table(c(list(Model=n,Cutoff=cutoffs[[n]]),as.list(measure(y[test_idx],probs_test[[n]],cutoffs[[n]]))))))
tab(cutoff_table[,.(Model,Cutoff,Accuracy,Precision,Recall,F1,TP,FP,FN)])
```

TP counts positive customers found correctly, TN counts negatives correctly rejected, FP counts unnecessary positive flags, and FN counts missed positives. At 0.50, `r winner` identifies `r test_table[Model==winner,TP]` positives and misses `r test_table[Model==winner,FN]`. Its recall is `r sprintf('%.2f',100*test_table[Model==winner,Recall])`%. This shows why selecting only the highest accuracy can leave many positive customers undiscovered.

The optional cutoffs maximize validation F1 over 0.01 to 0.80 in 0.01 steps. They are frozen before evaluation on test rows. At its selected cutoff of `r sprintf('%.2f',cutoffs[[winner]])`, `r winner` has `r sprintf('%.2f',100*cutoff_table[Model==winner,Recall])`% recall and `r sprintf('%.2f',100*cutoff_table[Model==winner,Precision])`% precision. A lower cutoff often finds more positives while adding false alarms. These cutoffs illustrate a tradeoff rather than a bank-approved operating policy. SVM calibration and cutoff selection share validation data, which can add optimism. Cutoffs do not change probabilities, AUC, or log loss.

```{r roc-graph}
# Sort each test forecast and compute exact cumulative ROC coordinates.
colors<-c('black','steelblue','darkorange3','firebrick')
plot(c(0,1),c(0,1),type='n',xlab='False positive rate',ylab='True positive rate',main='Common test ROC curves')
abline(0,1,lty=2,col='gray60')
for(i in seq_along(probs_test)) {
 p<-probs_test[[i]];ord<-order(p,decreasing=TRUE);yy<-y[test_idx][ord]
 ends<-which(!duplicated(p[ord],fromLast=TRUE))
 lines(c(0,cumsum(yy==0)[ends]/sum(yy==0),1),
       c(0,cumsum(yy==1)[ends]/sum(yy==1),1),col=colors[i],lwd=2)
}
legend('bottomright',paste(labels,'AUC',sprintf('%.3f',test_table$AUC)),col=colors,lwd=2,bty='n',cex=.8)
```

The ROC curves compare discrimination over all probability cutoffs. The horizontal axis shows the fraction of negatives incorrectly flagged, and the vertical axis shows the fraction of positives found. Curves closer to the upper-left corner have stronger separation. The diagonal is random ranking. The largest test AUC is `r sprintf('%.4f',max(test_table$AUC))` for `r test_table$Model[which.max(test_table$AUC)]`. AUC measures ordering, not calibration or a financial return.

# Training behavior and probability calibration

```{r learning-and-calibration}
# Show whether adding frozen boosting rounds transfers to validation rows.
history<-xgb_history
# Summarize and sort calibration groups before connecting their plotted points.
cal_rows<-list()
for(i in seq_along(probs_test)) {
 p<-probs_test[[i]];groups<-pmin(10,ceiling(rank(p,ties.method='first')/length(p)*10))
 b<-data.table(p=p,y=y[test_idx],group=groups)[,.(Predicted=mean(p),Observed=mean(y),Rows=.N),by=group]
 setorder(b,group);b[,Model:=names(probs_test)[i]];cal_rows[[i]]<-b
}
calibration_table<-rbindlist(cal_rows)
calibration_limit<-ceiling(10*max(calibration_table$Predicted,calibration_table$Observed))/10+.05
par(mfrow=c(1,2),mar=c(4,4,2,1))
matplot(seq_len(nrow(history)),history[,c('train_logloss','validation_logloss')],type='l',lty=1,
 col=c('black','firebrick'),xlab='Boosting round',ylab='Binary log loss',main='XGBoost learning')
legend('bottomleft',c('Training','Validation'),col=c('black','firebrick'),lty=1,bty='n',cex=.7)
# Use deciles of each model's own scores for a descriptive test calibration plot.
plot(c(0,calibration_limit),c(0,calibration_limit),type='n',xlab='Mean predicted probability',ylab='Observed positive fraction',main='Test calibration')
abline(0,1,lty=2,col='gray60')
for(i in seq_along(probs_test)) {
 b<-cal_rows[[i]]
 lines(b$Predicted,b$Observed,type='b',col=colors[i],pch=i,lwd=1.5)
}
legend('topleft',labels,col=colors,pch=1:4,lty=1,bty='n',cex=.7)
par(mfrow=c(1,1))
tab(data.frame(First_training_loss=history$train_logloss[1],Final_training_loss=tail(history$train_logloss,1),
 First_validation_loss=history$validation_logloss[1],Final_validation_loss=tail(history$validation_logloss,1)))
```

The learning plot tracks training and validation log loss as XGBoost adds trees. Training loss changes from `r sprintf('%.5f',history$train_logloss[1])` to `r sprintf('%.5f',tail(history$train_logloss,1))`; validation loss changes from `r sprintf('%.5f',history$validation_logloss[1])` to `r sprintf('%.5f',tail(history$validation_logloss,1))`. A widening gap indicates that additional fit is transferring less well to held-out observations. The round count remains the prior selected 600 even if the new sample's curve suggests a different choice. Retuning would be a separate experiment.

The calibration panel groups each model's test probabilities into ten equal-sized rank groups. Points near the diagonal indicate agreement between predicted and observed positive rates. A point above the line indicates underprediction; below it indicates overprediction. Grouping is descriptive and can hide within-group errors. It is not a formal statistical calibration test. This plot helps explain why the model with the best ranking need not also have the lowest probability cost.

In the highest-scoring XGBoost group, the mean predicted probability is `r sprintf('%.2f',100*calibration_table[Model=='XGBoost' & group==10,Predicted])`%, but `r sprintf('%.2f',100*calibration_table[Model=='XGBoost' & group==10,Observed])`% of customers are positive. That point sits well above the diagonal and shows underprediction. SVM's groups lie closer to the line overall, which is consistent with its lower test log loss. Logistic regression's highest group sits below the line, while the forest's highest group sits above it.

# Recommendation and limitations

For this controlled comparison, I would retain `r winner` as the probability-forecast benchmark because it has the lowest common test log loss. I would review its recall and false positives before choosing a cutoff for customer follow-up. The lowest loss is a measured result for these models, not evidence that one algorithm is universally best.

The model settings came from limited earlier searches and different selection criteria. All four were refitted on only 6,000 rows for a fair training-budget comparison, so stronger results may be possible with more data. In particular, the forest and XGBoost do not have their Week 5 training volumes. The SVM requires an extra calibration step, and its validation performance is consequently not independent of that step. A single common split does not measure sensitivity to sampling. Repeated splits or cross-validation, followed by a genuinely new final evaluation sample, would improve confidence in the recommendation.

The earlier course data were reused, the predictors are anonymized, and no monetary error costs or deployment constraints were provided. I would not interpret these results as proof of a business cause or as a ready-to-deploy decision policy. The useful finding is the measured difference in probability cost, discrimination, and threshold behavior under the same fitting and evaluation conditions.

# Reproducibility and sources

```{r execution-record}
# Save actual model outputs and row IDs so every reported number is auditable.
fwrite(test_table,file.path(results,'test_metrics.csv'))
fwrite(as.data.table(cost_table),file.path(results,'cost_comparison.csv'))
fwrite(cutoff_table,file.path(results,'selected_cutoff_metrics.csv'))
fwrite(rbindlist(cal_rows),file.path(results,'calibration_groups.csv'))
fwrite(data.table(ID_code=dat$ID_code[test_idx],target=y[test_idx],
 as.data.table(probs_test)),file.path(results,'test_predictions.csv'))
# Remove formula environments before saving to avoid serializing the entire
# analysis workspace through glm terms. This does not change predictions.
compact_glm<-function(m) {
 attr(m$terms,'.Environment')<-baseenv();environment(m$formula)<-baseenv()
 attr(m$model,'terms')<-NULL
 # The default binomial link is logit. Recreate its closures without retaining
 # an unevaluated link argument that can capture the entire knitting workspace.
 m$family<-stats::binomial();m
}
logistic_fit<-compact_glm(logistic_fit);calibration<-compact_glm(calibration)
models_to_save<-list(logistic=logistic_fit,svm=svm_fit,svm_calibration=calibration,forest=rf_fit,
 top50=top50,medians=med,centers=center,scales=spread,cutoffs=cutoffs,seed=seed)
saveRDS(models_to_save,file.path(results,'fitted_models.rds'))
saveRDS(list(signature=signature,models=models_to_save,
 margins=list(train=s_train,validation=s_val,test=s_test),history=xgb_history),cache_file)
xgb.save(xgb_fit,file.path(results,'xgboost.ubj'))
saveRDS(list(costs=cost_table,test=test_table,cutoff=cutoff_table,settings=settings,
 checks=checks,splits=split_table,winner=winner,history=history,
 calibration=coef(calibration)),file.path(results,'report_results.rds'))
write_json(list(costs=cost_table,test=test_table,cutoff=cutoff_table,settings=settings,
 checks=checks,splits=split_table,winner=winner,calibration=as.list(coef(calibration))),
 file.path(results,'summary.json'),pretty=TRUE,auto_unbox=TRUE,digits=12)
cat('All four selected models fitted and evaluated successfully.\n')
cat('Seed:',seed,'\nData MD5:',unname(tools::md5sum(data_path)),'\n')
print(sessionInfo())
```

The source R Markdown includes commented code for data checks, splitting, preprocessing, fitting, calibration, metrics, graphs, and saved outputs. The formal report hides source code for readability; the submitted R Markdown preserves it. All displayed findings come from the executed common-sample comparison.

Reruns can load the completed fits and SVM scores from a cache checked against the source file, input data, package versions, and partition IDs. Removing that cache forces the fitting code to run again. The first execution fitted all four models; caching only avoids repeating the same expensive calculations.

Sources are the Week 3 logistic regression report, both Week 4 SVM reports, and Week 5 ensemble report in this course's homework folders. Algorithm behavior is documented in the [R binomial family documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/family.html), the [e1071 package manual](https://stat.ethz.ch/CRAN/web/packages/e1071/e1071.pdf), [ranger documentation](https://imbs-hl.github.io/ranger/reference/ranger.html), and [XGBoost parameter documentation](https://xgboost.readthedocs.io/en/stable/parameter.html).
